title: Spacewalker
summary: A station crew is sent to check a failing gate while something strange stirs aboard.
html:
“Spacewalk. Report back to Head Sector. Over.”

“This is Spacewalk. I’ve nearly finished solar panel repairs. I fear left side may still be partially operational. Over.”

“Spacewalk. Report back to Head Sector ASAP. Do not delay. Over.”

The bays doors opened to consume the astronaut as he floated into the airlock. He pulled himself to the door and entered the main hall as the airlock slid open. A woman was waiting for him and lay against the opposite wall as he removed his helmet.

“Let’s go. They’re waiting for us in the Head,” she said.

“Wait – Nyles,” the astronaut protested.

“We don’t have time, Lancaster.”

“The solar panels.”

“I promise you, they can wait,” Nyles said. “We’re getting some kind of weird radiation readings. Nothing like we’ve seen before. Tony will explain it better than I can.”

The long hall was dimly lit by the occasional wall light, and the doors to the labs and living quarters were shut. They soon arrived in the darkened meeting room and were met by the rest of the crew. Dr. James Tony was gesturing to a screen on the ceiling as they entered the room. He noticed them and nodded politely.

“...We must then consider that saboteurs may try to damage the gates or open them early.”

“But what could they possibly gain from putting their own lives and the safety of humanity at risk?” one of the crew asked. “The gates are unstable enough as it is. Significant damage could be complete suicide.”

“Why haven’t we decommissioned them at this point?” Another crew member asked. “They’re a time bomb waiting to explode. There’s no chance we get the gates safely up and running in the next 30 years anyways.”

“You know as much as I do, Milton,” Dr. Tony responded. “Do you think IASA gives me any more information than any of you? We’ve tried to get them shut down. Last week, when Captain Tiller met with the Russians, they had asked the LFW to abort the program repeatedly. I don’t need to tell you how they responded.”

“Damn profit ghouls can’t let go of their pet projects, even if it risks us and the entire planet with us,” Milton grumbled.

“Welcome in, Lancaster,” Dr. Tony said. “I understand you’re quite passionate about keeping this ship in pristine condition, but we’ve received orders to keep all crew inside for a few hours.”

“With all due respect, sir: should another flare hit the panels again, I don’t know if we can keep running on battery power,” Lancaster said. “Some of the batteries are still damaged from the last flare.”

“I understand. Unfortunately the Command Center is not eager to lose an expensive employee to radiation,” Dr. Tony said. He gestured to the map on the screen above him. “As I was explaining, America Gate has been acting strangely. It’s possible that the previous flares have tampered with the satellite’s functioning, but we can’t be sure. WCC wants a team sent out to America Gate to check on it. The rest of us are to remain in the station and await further orders. As you may have heard, there are rumors of saboteurs on the other stations. Command Center worries that someone from the Asia or Euro stations may have been sent here to prevent the gates from firing. Or rather, I suppose, to keep them from opening the wormhole. They are possibly responsible for the early firing of the Euro Gate several days ago.”

“Again, what could they gain?” One of the crew asked. “If you plan to shut down the project, surely there are better ways to sabotage it. Firing a gate early risks hitting another station, or even your own. And now we know the energy that the beam unleashes, surely they wouldn’t want to risk another flare?”

“I don’t know, Alex. Someone must be very desperate.”

Nyles spoke up. “Thomson, Jackyll, Madison; you three are coming with me to the gate. The rest of you are to remain here at the station under Captain Sanderson. Sam Lancaster will work on repairing the nucs and getting the batteries fully operational again. Theo Milton and John Alex will assist Lancaster in the nuc room. You other five will retreat with Dr. Tony and Captain Sanderson to the crew quarters in case of radiation. Comms keep us in contact at all times, and prepare for emergency retrieval.”

Milton accosted Nyles as the crew dispersed. “Major Nyles,” he asked. “Why am I not going to the gate? I was one of the engineers on the original project. Surely my expertise is best served there?”

“You have been assigned to the nucs. We are all fully capable scientists and engineers in our own right. If we need assistance, we’ll call for you.”

“But, surely if you-”

“Lancaster, will the panels hold for at least 2 hours?”

“It is possible. But I really worry about the possibility of them giving out.”

“Possible is good enough. If Tony could explain…”

“Oh, of course,” Tony said. “Right. Before the previous flares, we detected radio waves that seemed to emanate from the target point. After the first, a burst of Hawking-like radiation was detected around the target point. Three bursts preceded the next flare, and a flash of light was seen at the target point immediately following the flare. On your walk to the solar panels, the dosimeters on your suit showed a concerning level of radiation over the twelve minutes you were out there, hence our decision to recall you inside. The gamma radiation levels are much higher than expected as we approach the target point, and there is serious concern of cosmic contamination. We will retain most astronauts in the station for the time being until we have completely passed the target point. Unfortunately, we have been commanded to send a team to check and repair the gate, but they are to return post-haste.”

Alex floated by with a box of tools under his arm. “Ready, Lancaster?”

“We need those batteries operational, because we can’t comfortably send another man out right now,” Dr. Tony said. “How quickly you think you can fix them?”

“The sooner we start, the better,” Lancaster replied.

“Right. Go ahead, then, boys.”

Lancaster and Alex navigated to the nuc bay and donned maintenance suits. Once safely suited, they entered the bay through the airlock. The battery room was barely lit by the overhead lights and the glow of computer screens.

“Where’s Milton?” Lancaster asked.

“Beats me,” Alex replied. “He should have got here by now. Perhaps Major Nyles is still chewing his ass out in Headquarters.”

Lancaster chuckled. “BMS shows a few loss connections and a loose wire. Seems to be up towards your end.”

“There’s some visual bruising, but diagnostics don’t detect any leaks,” Alex said. “No chemical contamination here.”

“A1 and C3 don’t show up. I wouldn’t lose the suit just yet, Johnny. Both modules are shorted, minimum, probably seriously damaged. Help me replace these.”

The men pulled the faulty modules from the battery rack and dragged them into the storage room to swap them with working batteries. Once swapped, Lancaster returned to storage and examined the broken batteries for cracks or leaking. The radio at his side crackled to life.

“Station A ejecting travel pod. Destination: Gate A. Requesting permission. Over.”

“Station A. This is Charleston. Route to Gate A clear for passage. Over.”

“Thank you, Charleston. Launching in 5… 4… 3… 2… 1… Charleston, travel pod bound for Gate A. Over.”

“Travel pod deployed,” the ship’s intercom announced. “Estimated return time, 35 minutes. All crew on emergency standby.”

Lancaster taped over the cracks in the casing and tied them down on the storage rack. When he left storage, Alex had removed his helmet and was lying sideways with his head shoved inside the access panel to the rear of the battery rack.

“The wires are tight. We should be good to go,” Alex said. “Run a test from BMS, will you?”

“Where’s your helmet, Johnny?”

“Diagnostics said we’re clear from contaminants. How we looking now?”

Lancaster checked the console. “Connections good. Batteries charging. Incoming power is weaker than I’d like, but we’re down a few solar panels, so it is what it is.”

Alex pulled himself out and latched the access panel. “We should be passing behind the earth shortly, might be a few minutes before the solar panels get sunlight again. Do we have enough?”

“Six batteries full, two batteries a quarter charged. It should last us, God permitting.”

“And where the hell is Milton? Shouldn’t he be here by now?”

“That’s a good-”

The station violently rocked, and Lancaster felt a wall slam into his back. He floated for a moment before recovering and grasping a handhold on the wall. The room plunged into darkness and the ship went nearly silent. A faint whirring echoed through the halls as the station struggled to life again. Lancaster lay against the wall as the room spun around him. A flashlight shone into his eyes, and he winced.

“Damn it, you’re alive.”

“I will murder you, Johnny.”

Alex chuckled. “No, no. It’s good you’re okay. They’d have my hide if I let my boss die on assignment.”

“Oh. So now I’m your boss. But when I send you with Madison to check the batteries-”

Alex shoved him back against the wall and floated past him. “Alright, boss. Speaking of batteries…”

“BMS is down,” Lancaster said, maneuvering to the blackened screen. The whole station is on life support. Damn! We were barely holding on as it was.”

“The batteries had juice, Right?” Alex said. “I don’t see any major damage. If we shift electricity output, maybe there’s enough to power the essentials.”

“Cut off the halls, lab, and quarters lights. We’ll need power for the BMS, essential comms, and airflow.” Lancaster went to the access panel and peaked inside. “Pass me a light.”

“Uh, Sam?”

“Pass me a light, man. What on earth…”

Lancaster turned around and saw a faint light glowing in the entrance to the battery room. A bright little creature stood in the entrance, its sides lit with a soft gray glow that lit up the dark room. It was a flat creature, low to the ground, with some number of tentacle-like legs that folded under its body. It waddled across the floor, up the far wall, and across the ceiling towards them before vanishing; then reappeared at the entrance to the room and once again moved across the room; over and over again taking the same path towards them until it vanished and started the journey from the beginning. Up it came and across the ceiling until it got to where the men expected for it to vanish again. But this time, it stopped. Alex shakily lifted his light to shine on the creature, which promptly exploded in a ball of flame that lit the dark room in a flash, blinding the men.

Lancaster blinked slowly and covered his eyes from the light. He felt pain radiating down the back of his head and neck, and he felt as if he had fallen head-first against a brick wall. The scene around him spun dizzyingly as he struggled to lift his head from the ground. Something large overshadowed him, and he slid his hand to his side and looked up through squinted eyes. Snake-like appendages hovered about him, and a low humming rumbled the ground beneath him. Then the light was gone, and he was floating through the dark station, his head reeling, and his stomach unsettled.

He was in the main hall. The door to the lab was open, and a glow emanated from within. He spun slowly to see the door to the crew quarters open also. Someone was lying near motionless near the floor, and Lancaster moved to his side.

“Dr. Tony?” Lancaster shook him gently. “Dr. Tony!”

The man seemed unconscious, breathing painfully. Lancaster felt the blood on his hand and saw the red-stained coat that he wore. He pulled off the man’s coat and lifted his shirt. A shallow but bloody gash cut across his left side, and his chest was purple throughout with bruising.

“C’mon, man.” Lancaster pulled Dr. Tony onto a nearby bed and looked around. He found a medical kit in one of the emergency compartments under the beds and cleaned the wound quickly. Dr. Tony started and stared at Lancaster in shock. Lancaster smiled grimly and continued wrapping his torso.

“Might feel a bit tight.”

“Another flare? Nyles and the crew… They were… *cough* They were out there…”

“Was the rest of the crew with them?”

Tony stared at Lancaster blankly.

“The crew. Where are they? Weren’t they with you here?”

“… They ought to be.”

“Then where the hell…?”

Tony looked out the dim doorway into the station hall. The little disc creature was sitting on the side of the open door frame. It crawled along the wall towards the two men until it was within a meter or so of the bed. Both men froze, waiting for something to happen. The creature extended its legs and pushed off the wall, floating across the room until it hit the opposite wall and vanished. Lancaster closed the first aid kit and pulled Tony’s shirt over the bandages.

“I think they opened the gates, Sam,” Tony whispered despairingly.

Lancaster shook his head vigorously. “Nonsense. The gates weren’t ready. We weren’t ready. After the flares, and the damage to America Gate, We- they couldn’t.”

A flash of light engulfed the room and Lancaster was jerked forward onto the floor. He reeled from the blow to his head as he drifted up from the floor. As he recovered, he felt someone shaking him.

“Wake up, Lancaster.”

“I’m alive, Theo,” he responded. “Dr. Tony. Are you OK?”

Tony groaned.

“Good enough,” Milton said. “C’mon, Lancaster. I’m getting a signal from the travel pod. They need us in headquarters.”

Lancaster glanced back at Tony still floating by the bed.

“Go on,” Tony said.

The hall lights flickered pathetically from the lab and quarters all the way to headquarters. They passed a window on their way to headquarters, and Lancaster saw a body floating out into space away from the ship. “What happened to him?”

“I wouldn’t keep staring,” Milton said, pulling on his sleeve. “It doesn’t get prettier.”

At the end of the corridor, the sliding door to headquarters slid back and forth on its track, trying to close despite the metal bar blocking the way. Milton grabbed the door and pulled it open, and the two men floated into the room, navigating to the dashboard of flickering lights and feebly glowing panels.

“Travel Pod, this is Station A. Are you with us, Travel Pod?”

“Here.” The voice crackled. “The pod is offline. We have no way to make it to the gates. No way to get back.”

“Wait.” Lancaster grabbed the mic. “If the pod is offline, how are you transmitting to us?”

Milton pulled him away from the panel. “Travel Pod. How far are you from Gate A?”

“1.3 kilometers, at closest.” The pod answered.

“Theo,” Lancaster interjected. “How are they contacting us if the pod is online?”

Milton glared at him, and Lancaster felt a shiver run down his spine. The room spun briefly, and Lancaster thought he saw movement in the corner of his eye. He looked back at the doorway behind them. Dr. Tony stood in the doorway, blood seeping through his shirt and staining his coat. It rose up his chest until he was drooling pale red blood that drifted away from his face in crimson droplets. A dark mist rolled down the hall and enveloped Tony and he slowly melted away. Lancaster gasped as his awareness returned to him. “… As far… Try… return to the ship, get the gate online if possible.” Milton was sending orders to the astronauts in the pod. The pod. The pod was damaged and out of power. The pod-

“Theo.”

Milton ignored him. “Three meters to the gate. You can send Thomson out. The hatch to the airlock is above the battery compartment. Get it, get to the override panel.”

“Roger. Thomson is a go,” the response came.

“Major Nyles. How long until we hit the next breach?”

“2 minutes 46 seconds.”

“Theo!”

“What?” Milton shot back.

“If they can transmit, they must have some power in the ship. They can make it back.”

“They are at the gate, already,” Milton responded. He turned back to the comms. “Travel Pod. How close are we to discharge?”

“T-minus 330 seconds.”

“We don’t have that much time. You have to speed things up.”

“T-minus 240 seconds.”

“Again.”

“This tech is below what-”

“Again.”

“What are you doing, Theo?” Lancaster demanded. He moved toward the mic, but some kind of force slammed into his chest and threw him against the opposite wall. Milton turned his head without moving his body and glared at Lancaster.

“We don’t have time,” he said.

Lancaster tried to pry off the invisible hands that clutched his throat as Milton instructed the members aboard the travel pod. Feeling the grasp loosen, he pulled himself along the wall and towards the exit hall. Dr Tony appeared in front of him, blocking the hall.

His eyes, hollow and black, stood out against his pale face spattered with blood. “You can’t leave yet,” he said softly.

Lancaster backed away and glanced at Milton, who turned his head back to look at him without pausing his work.

“We’re nearly out of time. Thomson. Status?”

“Ready to fire, Station A.”

“15 seconds. Major Nyles.”

“Already on standby.”

The monitor above the comms panel lit up and showed a map with the earth at its center. The markers the gates were arranged neatly in a nearly equilateral triangle around the earth. The white dotted line connecting the gates flashed green for a moment, then one of the gates began flashing red.

“Gate C is drifting off course. Failure pending.”

“Fire now!” Milton shouted.

“Roger. Gate A firing off.”

New voices came in through the speaker.

“Gate B firing off.”

“Gate C firing off.”

Total silence. A deafening roar and a flash of light. Lancaster fell to the floor and watched in a daze as Milton dissolved into a cloud of darkness before everything went dark.

“Sam! Wake up, man!”

Lancaster groaned moved his arm. “Ugh.” He winced. “Milton. What...?” He bumped against the window next to him and gathered that he was in the lab.

“Where have you been?” Milton asked. “John says you straight up vanished after that big flare.”

“I went with you. The comms, the travel pods…”

“The hell you on about? I’ve been in the nuc bay with Johnny. I haven’t seen you since the power went out.”

“Huh?” Lancaster grabbed onto the wall to rest. “Theo, I’ve been with you at head sector. We were talking to the travel pod and…”

“The travel pod is gone.” Milton stared at Lancaster disbelievingly. “They were destroyed in the flare that took out the power.”

“That’s impossible… We were just talking to them…”

“Oh, you’re still alive!” Alex met the two men there in the hall. “I though you were lost, man.”

“He’s been hallucinating,” Milton said. “He must have hit his head pretty bad.”

Lancaster spun around. “Milton, you know damn well we were both at head sector! What in the hell is going on here?”

“Who are you talking to?” Milton asked.

Lancaster looked back at him next to Alex, and forward at the doorway where he was standing, watching the three of them. “I- I am talking to you…”

The man in front of them took a step forward. The dim red emergency lights shone clearly on an uncanny, almost inhuman mimicry of the face and features of Theo Milton. The three men glanced at each other, and back at the eerie man standing still in the doorway, as if on solid ground. Suddenly, all three were spun by an unseen force to face the open window behind them. Portals rent space outside the window and ushered an unknown dimension into our world. The station window looked down upon the planet below, where sparks of flaming meteors fell through the atmosphere. There was a flash in the Mediterranean, and another over north Africa. Rifts appeared in space all around the planet, and meteors flowed out of them and into the atmosphere. A wave of fire tens of thousands of miles wide swept across Europe.

Lancaster tried to turn his head to look behind him, but to no avail. The sun set behind the earth while the planet lit up with the light of a million fires.
